title: Night People and ’90s New York
summary: Mark Ronson looks back on becoming a DJ in 1990s New York, carrying records across the city and learning in rooms shaped by hip-hop history.
transcript:
Mark Ronson spoke with Simon, via video link to the Triple R studios, around the September 2025 release of his memoir Night People: How to Be a DJ in '90s New York City (Grand Central Publishing). Edited for length and clarity.

Simon: Firstly, a huge honour and a great pleasure to speak with you, and congratulations on the book. We received a copy, and all I've been doing all week is immersing myself in the 90s world you're portraying.

Mark: It's very nice to look into a radio studio and see a Technics turntable right behind you, as well.

Simon: We've got some Pioneers too. But before we start, I wanted to pass on best wishes from Chris Gill, who runs Northside Records here.

Mark: Oh yeah, Chris, of course.

Simon: He has a show here called Get Down.

Mark: No, I know. I think I've listened to it online a few times, too.

Simon: Lots of strong Melbourne connections. But I wanted to start with one aspect of the book. I know you've said it's a little tongue-in-cheek, how to be a DJ in 1990s New York City, as far as how-to guides go. But at the same time, you're recognising there's something very valuable in preserving a specific set of knowledge: the fundamentals. Can you tell us about the importance of that aspect of the book to you?

Mark: I really try not to be one of those people who's ever: it was better then, or the DJing then was more serious, or you had to work harder because you were collecting vinyl, all these things. But it's true, it's nice to preserve it either way. Even when I DJ vinyl now, and I'm no A-Trak, some wizard turntablist, I've been playing a lot of vinyl hip hop sets lately, and when kids come, they're just mesmerised. There's an entire generation of people who've never seen someone throw records on and off, mix eight bars, drop records on vinyl, and the chaotic vinyl ballet that entails. So I wasn't looking to say this was the best kind of DJing, but I wanted to write about it because I didn't know anybody else who had, and I wanted to celebrate some of the great DJs, the people who were influential for me. And there are certain, not lessons, because I don't think of myself as a teacher, but certain things you could take away from the book that would be universal in any era. A lot of it is me saying: this is the 90s. This isn't the DJ how-to book if you're starting up now. If you're starting up now, you should get a controller, and of course you should. But there are other rules, like don't play the big records before the opener, and don't repeat records, all these things I learned coming up that are in this book and would still apply to anyone today.

Simon: There's a tremendous generosity in that. And watching your TED Talk, where you're tracing the origins of certain samples and the language of hip hop, it's a beautiful thing to pass that on generationally. This book feels like part of that conversation.

Mark: Yeah, I think so. There are probably things that DJs and producers who came up in my era just take as given: the way we used to dig for samples and look for breaks. I forget sometimes, when I say those things, that to some of this generation their minds are blown. Like: wait, there was a record convention in a hotel in Times Square that you had to go to to get the rarest breaks. And if there was a record I really wanted to hear, like the sample from my favourite hip hop record of that era, 'They Reminisce Over You', which was a sample from Tom Scott: I only knew one person who had that record. So if I wanted to hear it, I had to go to their room at the university and wait for them to come home, like a junkie, fiending to hear it. Something very provincial and sweet, and, I guess, interesting, about that time.

Simon: Things move so quickly that it's important to pause and reflect on how far things have come, even as some things remain the same.

Mark: Yeah. The sacredness or the sanctity of the music will always stay the same. It's just the different ways that we get it. In the book, I really wanted to stay in the diaristic nature of the 90s, so it's only in the epilogue that I come out to draw comparisons between now, the Serato and USB sticks, and vinyl. And there are moments where I have to be honest and say: I did like the fact that, bringing 300 of your records to work every night, you were turning this soulless closet, or DJ booth, or the corner of the room where the turntables were, into basically a mini pop-up museum. We didn't think about it back then, because that's just what we did every night. But now you think about it: how much life it brings when you're carrying your treasures around all the time.

Simon: And there's a really beautiful section about how you even managed the logistics of moving all that vinyl from your apartment to the —

Mark: Oh man, it was crazy. A lot of the time there were five flights of stairs; I lived in this walk-up on Franklin Street. If I was playing a hot club, my friends would volunteer to come and help me, but if I was playing some place that wasn't the spot, sometimes I'd just be carrying that stuff myself. And in the one place that actually had an elevator, which I talk about in the book, there was this thing of trying to get three crates in: leaving one in the front door, taking the second one and putting that in the elevator door to keep it open, getting the third one and throwing that in the elevator, going back for the first one in the door, kicking the one in the door inside, and then having to do the whole thing in reverse. You had already broken a sweat before you were in the cab to the gig.

Simon: A physical and mental challenge. You're in prime condition by the end of it.

Mark: Yeah. And I've been DJing so much with vinyl the last six months, and my back is so messed up again. I'm like, man, I don't know how I used to just carry this up and down stairs into basements all the time. But it also is a lot of fun.

Simon: Thrilled to hear it. Not about your back, but that it's been a lot of fun. Maybe we can shift into the world you're presenting in the book. It starts in 1993 and proceeds through the decade. For people who haven't had a chance to read it yet, or hear the songs you're referencing, can you paint a picture of what your day-to-day was like?

Mark: So, 93 till about 96, that's when I'm starting off. I was a 17-year-old kid when I started DJing, just hustling to get gigs, opening for anybody. And my hero was Stretch Armstrong, this legendary New York radio and club DJ. I essentially kind of stalked him, and I would steal his mixes, not realising that was blatantly wrong. I eventually got a few gigs opening for him, but then I had some setbacks and rubbed a few promoters the wrong way, probably because I was biting Stretch's mixes. By the mid-90s I had a little party on a Tuesday called Sweet Thang, and that's when I started to make a name for myself. Underground heroes like Gang Starr came, but then Biggie started coming down, and one night Biggie brought Jay-Z, and Fat Joe brought Big Pun another night. So it was starting to get like: wow, these real kings of the radio and the clubs were coming. I made my name then. And then it was the late 90s in New York when bottle service came and the music got a little more commercial, and Puffy really took over New York City, and the scene became more blingy. But I was also the DJ of choice. So even though you could argue the scene was a bit superficial, here I am in the room playing 'Hard Knock Life' while Jay-Z is ten feet from me, and the whole club's singing off-key: it's a hard knock life. It was incredible. I was 23 in 1999. To be DJing for these guys, for the heroes, even as the scene was maybe shifting to a slightly more commercial place: I didn't have that hindsight back then. I was just like, oh my god, here I am, I'm in the right rooms, rocking these crowds and having the best time.

Simon: As a producer, this is a bit of an aside, but you're very well known for bringing over a classic sound with a modern punch. Is that coming from your perspective as a DJ, working out what's going to move the floor?

Mark: There's definitely something inextricably linked to all my years of DJing. As a DJ, if you play a lot of different genres in your set and figure out how to mix them together, which I was doing by the end of the 90s, playing Biggie but also AC/DC and Rufus and Chaka Khan, you see music as a thing where a lot of elements can coexist. So I've always had that, for better or for worse, that sense of blending genres in the music I make. The first record I ever got to produce was for Nikka Costa, who, at the time I met her, was an Australian artist, on Mushroom, even though she was from the States. I got that gig because her manager liked the way I put all these different things together. She had this brilliant voice, and they were like: hey, I think our record should sound like a mix of AC/DC, Rufus and Chaka Khan, and Biggie. But yes, absolutely, as a DJ you do get a good sense of what makes people move. And then there's the adverse time, it's not as often, where I have to shut off the spinning disco ball in my head, because there's a beautiful ballad and you don't want to ruin it with some banging drums or something. The DJ thing has been such a huge influence on all my production.

Simon: Nice to hear a couple of Melbourne references in there, including AC/DC, which you've mentioned as a bit of a eureka moment: realising you could blend the urgency of those rock records into your hip hop and funk sets.

Mark: Yes, it really was. And through Nikka, through that connection, is how I met Daniel Merriweather and heard about him. So I've always had a really strong Melbourne connection. Melbourne just has such a great scene: going to Northside, even just the local Melbourne releases from that week. I picked up so many records from Chris, because there was so much great stuff.

Simon: It's funny, I think one of the records you picked up was from Harvey Sutherland: Boy, the one with his portrait on the cover. He actually came in yesterday; he's got a new album on the way.

Mark: I love it. I DM'd with him afterwards, just telling him how much I dug it. And I love the cover almost as much as I like the music; it's so iconic. It reminded me of The Nightfly, Donald Fagen, or something. Just brilliant.

Simon: That's really cool. Coming back to the book: the process of writing it is really interesting, because you're familiar with the work involved in preparing a set, or making a record, or doing a soundtrack, but this is very different, and I think it took longer than anything you've done before. Over three years, is that right?

Mark: Yeah, it took me three years. I took time out in the middle because we were working on the Barbie film, but it really did eat my life in a different way. And I hadn't thought about it until somebody said it to me last week, but everything else I've done is pretty much collaborative, and this is the only thing that was really just me, with, obviously, the assistance of some brilliant editors. The first year I was plugging away, and the writing was bad. I've seen it. I asked my editor: how did you not flag that this is terrible? He said: I had faith that you would find it. But there was still this sense that I've never written anything before. When I'm working on a song, I have a pretty good idea, a little bit into the process: is this any good? Is this worth keeping on? I didn't have that knowledge with the book. I just had to trust: okay, I'm this deep in it, I'd better keep going. But it did consume even more than music, because even when I'm working on a record I'm in love with, I have to go to the studio to do it, and you can write anywhere. At the end of the book, the last three months, I was waiting for my wife, Grace, to fall asleep and then crawling out of bed to spend another two, three hours, because I just had to finish at that point. So yes, it was really all-consuming, but then also incredibly fulfilling creatively.

Simon: I love that picture of having to sneak every second. Maybe to finish: writing this book has enabled you to revisit that time. Are there things you've learned about yourself in the process, or things you see differently now, with the benefit of hindsight?

Mark: There's a lot. Writing can be an incredibly self-involved thing, because you're basically having, in some ways, a five-hour therapy session every day. You're thinking about all these things that you did, and mistakes, and things along the way that were signposts for where you were going. I had a little bit of success early, halfway through the 90s, but there were a lot of stumbles and falls, and I really wanted to make music and be taken seriously as a producer and a songwriter. So DJing was always this funny tangent, but not what I was chasing. Even when I had success there, it wasn't like: I've set out to do this thing and it's happening. And it was really lovely to reconnect with all those people; I interviewed 150, maybe 200 people for this book. And, let's be honest, for people working nightlife it's not the easiest exit. Not everyone's had the best life. I saw it during COVID, with so many of my DJ friends having medical GoFundMes and all this stuff. But yeah, I did learn a lot. I didn't set out to write such a personal book, with all the addiction and compulsion stuff. But I realised that if you call the book Night People, and you're trying to figure out why we all went out at night and what we were chasing or running from, you have to talk about some demons as well.

Simon: It's a tremendous book: so well written, and so illuminating. And for the many of us who are huge fans, it's such a gift to receive. Thank you.

Mark: I really appreciate it. Thank you so much.

Simon: I should let you go for your next interview, but congratulations again, and hopefully we'll see you in Melbourne before too long.

Mark: I hope so too.

Simon: Take care.

pullQuote.text: The sacredness or the sanctity of the music will always stay the same. It's just the different ways that we get it.
pullQuote.speaker: Mark Ronson
